area: Area VI. Flight by Reference to Instruments
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why pitch holds the airspeed while the power stays set, teach entries into straight and turning climbs and descents from cruise or climb and descent speed, the stabilized climb and descent, and the level-offs with the IFH leads, on round dials and on glass, full panel and partial panel, fly them from the right seat while explaining them, and analyze and correct the common errors an examiner simulates.
why: Climbs and descents are where pitch, power and trim all change together, and the IFH lists eleven common faults for straight climbs and descents alone [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Every IFR flight needs them: when ATC has not said "at pilot's discretion" or set a restriction, pilots climb or descend at an optimum rate to 1,000 feet from the assigned altitude, then at 500 to 1,500 fpm, and advise ATC if unable to manage at least 500 fpm [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]. Without the attitude indicator, the airspeed, altimeter and VSI show varying rates of change through the transition to a descent [[23:177|IFH 7-16]], which is why the PTS wants this Area taught partial panel too (CFII PTS, Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills).

warmup: Think first: your student enters a climb from cruise and the airspeed settles 10 knots below the POH climb speed while the VSI shows a healthy 900 fpm. She is pleased with the rate. Which instrument should she be flying the pitch by, what will the rate do when she fixes the speed, and how would you explain it so it sticks?

key_terms.def: Climb power set and held; pitch holds the airspeed. Once stable the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch and the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge is the primary power instrument [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
The Task E method: once the rate settles, the VSI is primary for pitch and the airspeed indicator primary for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
For a given power setting and load, the one attitude that gives the most efficient rate of climb; the POH/AFM gives the airspeed and climb power that set it [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
The same attitude gives different performance with different power and airplanes: 500 fpm at 90 knots in a small airplane, 2,000 fpm at 250 knots in a jet [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].
At constant power the airspeed shows pitch: nose lower, speed up; nose higher, speed down; a rapid change means a large pitch change [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].
Starting the level-off before the altitude; for climbs, 10 percent of the vertical speed, so 50 feet at 500 fpm and 100 feet at 1,000 fpm [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].
Reducing power before cruise speed is reached on a level-off; the amount depends on how fast the airplane accelerates [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:209|IFH 7-48]].
Letting the nose pitch up on a level-off from a descent, from not holding the descending attitude with forward pressure as power is added [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].
The trend on the PFD airspeed tape showing where the airspeed will be in 6 seconds; it helps judge pitch corrections and the power lead [[23:198|IFH 7-37]] [[23:209|IFH 7-48]].
Trim works on airflow, so it is a function of speed; an airplane trimmed in pitch seeks its trim speed, and any change in airspeed needs a trim adjustment [[23:85|IFH 4-8]] [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].
Flying with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative, or on glass with the AHRS simulated or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]] [[23:194|IFH 7-33]].
An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can feel like tumbling backward; the disoriented pilot may push abruptly nose-low [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: What this Task adds, and how it is tested

body.p: **Teaching constant airspeed climbs and descents** builds on Tasks A and C. The lesson FII.VI.A already covers the two methods, how to recognize and simulate instrument failures, the positive exchange of controls and the straight-and-level error lists; FII.VI.C covers power changes, trim and speed changes in turns. This lesson does not repeat them. Here the focus is pitch holding an airspeed while the power stays set, entries from two speeds, and level-offs with the right lead.

The idea in one line: once the climb is stable, the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch and the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge is the primary power instrument; if the airspeed is low or high, make a small pitch correction [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. In a constant rate climb or descent the roles change: the VSI becomes primary for pitch and the airspeed indicator primary for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. That is Task E. Application: expect students to mix the two, and have them name the method before every climb or descent.

check.q: The examiner asks: "In this Task, what tells your student the pitch is right, and what tells her the power is right?" Answer in one breath.
check.a: Once stable, the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch, and the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge is the primary power instrument, monitored to make sure climb power is held [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. In a constant airspeed descent, any airspeed deviation calls for a pitch adjustment [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Power, attitude and airspeed: the logic of the maneuver

body.p: **Power and attitude equal performance.** In the IFH example a small airplane at full power, with the miniature aircraft two bar widths above the horizon, climbs at 500 fpm and 90 knots; the same picture in a jet gives 2,000 fpm and 250 knots [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. The picture alone does not tell a student what the airplane will do. She has to know the numbers for her airplane.

For a given power setting and load there is only one attitude that gives the most efficient rate of climb, and the POH/AFM gives the airspeed and climb power that set it [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Those speeds are based on maximum gross weight, so pilots must know how they vary with weight [[23:207|IFH 7-46]]. How steeply the airplane climbs depends on excess thrust: with none it flies level, and with a deficit it descends [[23:87|IFH 4-10]].

**Why the airspeed is the pitch instrument.** At constant power the airspeed indicator shows pitch indirectly: as the nose lowers the airspeed increases, as it rises the airspeed decreases, and a rapid change means a large pitch change [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]. Power is fixed in this maneuver, so the airspeed becomes the pitch reference. The same logic shows in a trimmed airplane: after even a slight power reduction the nose drops just enough to hold the trimmed airspeed, and the airplane descends at a rate directly proportionate to the thrust removed [[24:369|AFH 18-20]].

callout.text: Constant airspeed: pitch holds the speed, power sets the rate. Constant rate: pitch holds the rate, power holds the speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[24:369|AFH 18-20]].

check.q: Your student in a stabilized constant airspeed climb sees the airspeed 5 knots low with a good climb rate, and reaches for the throttle. What do you teach?
check.a: Power stays at the climb setting, and the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch: a low airspeed calls for an appropriately small pitch correction, nose down [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Adding power to fix the airspeed while holding the vertical speed is the constant rate technique [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

chunks.title: Entering the climb on round dials, from cruise or climb speed

body.p: **Procedure using full panel for an entry into a straight climb from cruising airspeed** [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]:

bullets: Raise the miniature aircraft to the approximate nose-high indication for the climb speed. The attitude varies with the type of airplane [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Apply light back pressure to start and hold the climb attitude. The pressures change as the airplane slows [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Advance the power to the climb setting, either with the pitch change or after the pitch is set and the airspeed approaches climb speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Watch the VSI: after a smooth transition it shows an immediate upward trend, keeps moving slowly, then stops at a rate that fits the stabilized airspeed and attitude [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Hold heading and trim as in straight-and-level flight [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

body.p: Figure 7-25 tags the attitude indicator as supporting pitch and bank, the VSI as supporting pitch, the turn coordinator as supporting bank, the heading indicator as primary bank and the power gauges as primary power. It tags no primary pitch instrument for the entry [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Application: during the entry the student sets an attitude on the attitude indicator and lets the speed come to it; the airspeed takes over as primary once it is stable.

**Procedure from climbing airspeed.** First complete the slowdown from cruise to climb speed in straight-and-level flight (Task C). The climb entry is then the same as from cruise, except that power goes up to the climb setting at the same time as the pitch is raised [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Climb entries on partial panel are more easily and accurately controlled from climbing speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

**Entry into a climbing turn.** Combine the straight climb technique with the turn technique, allow for the effects on lift and power, and speed up the cross-check to cover bank as well as pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. For visual climbing turns the AFH allows two ways: enter the climb first and then bank, or climb and turn at the same time, with shallow banks so the climb stays efficient [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

**Coordination and trim on entry.** Added power makes a single-engine airplane yaw and roll left unless aileron and rudder counter it, and keeping ahead takes a faster cross-check [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. As the pitch rises, P-factor and torque add to the left yaw and roll, so right rudder and aileron pressure are needed [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Trim is a function of speed, so slowing from cruise to climb speed needs a retrim [[23:85|IFH 4-8]].

callout.text: Application: from cruise the IFH lets power go in with the pitch change or after it [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Pick one and teach it the same way every time, visually and under the hood, so the student's hands learn one sequence.

check.q: Your student enters a climb from climb speed by raising the nose first and adding power several seconds later. What will she see, and what does the IFH say?
check.a: From climbing airspeed, power goes up at the same time as the pitch is raised [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Power added after the pitch change shows a decrease in airspeed from the added drag [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

chunks.title: On a PFD: entering and holding the climb

body.p: **Procedure using full panel on an electronic flight display, from cruise airspeed.** Slowly and smoothly apply aft pressure to raise the yellow chevron until its tip points to the desired degree of pitch. Hold the pressure and smoothly add climb power, either before starting the pitch change or once the pitch is set. Consult the POH/AFM for climb power if anything other than a full power climb is wanted [[23:207|IFH 7-46]].

As the airspeed decreases the control forces grow; trim them off so the pitch holds without constant attention and the scan can stay wide [[23:207|IFH 7-46]]. The VSI tape should trend up at once and settle on a rate that matches the pitch and power, a rate that changes with weight and atmospheric conditions [[23:207|IFH 7-46]] [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

**From an established climb airspeed.** Slow to climb speed in level flight first; the entry is the same except that power is increased when the pitch is raised. Power added after the pitch change shows a decrease in airspeed from the increased drag; power added before it makes the airspeed increase from the excess thrust [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

**Stabilized on the PFD.** The ASI is the primary pitch instrument, the heading indicator the primary bank instrument, and the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge the primary power instrument. If the pitch is right, the airspeed slowly decreases to the target; if not, make small pitch changes until it stabilizes. Any change in airspeed requires a trim adjustment [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. The airspeed trend indicator shows where the speed will be in 6 seconds [[23:198|IFH 7-37]], a quick way to see whether a pitch change is working.

On glass, the attitude indicator is primary only when flying a specific pitch or bank angle; otherwise it is a control instrument [[23:199|IFH 7-38]]. Application: during the entry the student flies a target pitch on the chevron, then hands primary pitch to the airspeed tape once the speed settles. For corrections, 1° of pitch is a fifth of the chevron's thickness [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

In a climbing turn the turn rate indicator is primary for bank in a standard-rate turn, since it is the only instrument that can show standard rate; the attitude indicator sets the bank and supports [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

callout.text: Figure 7-64's tags (primary pitch at the top of the altitude tape, primary power at the airspeed tape, supporting power at the manifold pressure gauge) are not the stabilized-climb primaries in the text on the same page [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. They match the level-flight set the IFH gives when slowing from 120 to 100 knots at 18 inches [[23:201|IFH 7-40]], and the figure shows 100 knots at 4,000 feet with 18.0 inches and 1,800 rpm, so read it as the slowdown that starts this entry. Teach the text for the climb itself: once stable, the airspeed tape is primary for pitch and the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge for power [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

check.q: On a PFD your student sets the climb pitch from cruise, and the airspeed settles 6 knots above climb speed. What does she do?
check.a: Small pitch changes until the airspeed stabilizes at the desired speed [[23:208|IFH 7-47]], for example 1°, a fifth of the chevron, the size the IFH uses for small altitude corrections [[23:197|IFH 7-36]], then trim, since any change in airspeed requires a trim adjustment [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

chunks.title: The stabilized climb, straight and turning

body.p: **A stabilized straight climb.** Once the airplane is steady at a constant airspeed and attitude, the ASI is primary for pitch and the heading indicator stays primary for bank. Monitor the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge as the primary power instrument to make sure climb power is still set. If the attitude is right for the power, the airspeed stabilizes at the target; if it is low or high, make an appropriately small pitch correction [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Figures 7-26 and 7-27 make a good side-by-side for the student: the same panel, but in the constant rate climb the VSI is tagged primary for pitch and the ASI primary for power [[23:176|IFH 7-15]].

**Climb power does not hold itself.** A normally aspirated engine loses power as altitude increases: RPM falls with a fixed-pitch propeller and manifold pressure with a controllable propeller, so the pilot keeps advancing the throttle to hold the climb setting [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. The rate the airplane settles at depends on weight and atmospheric conditions [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. Under IFR, if the airplane cannot climb at least 500 fpm, advise ATC [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]].

**A stabilized climbing turn.** Combine the climb with the turn and speed up the cross-check for bank as well as pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. At constant power the airplane cannot hold the same pitch and airspeed in a bank as in a straight climb: it climbs at a slightly shallower angle because some lift is turning it, and steep banks cut the rate of climb a lot [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

bullets: Bank for standard rate is about 15 percent of true airspeed: divide by 10 and add half the result, about 15° at 100 knots [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. IFH 4-11 gives a second rule, airspeed ÷ 10 plus 7, which gives 16° at 90 knots [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]; FII.VI.B compares the two.
Set the bank on the attitude indicator, then use the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft as primary for bank, the attitude indicator supporting [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
Check the ball throughout, especially if pressures are held rather than trimmed off [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
Roll out at the same rate as the roll-in and lead the heading by half the bank; the attitude indicator is primary for bank during the roll-out, the heading indicator once level [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
Do not stare at the heading indicator: in a 90° turn at standard rate it can be left out of the cross-check for about 20 seconds [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

callout.text: Application: in a climbing turn the airspeed, not the altimeter, tells the student whether the pitch is right. The level-turn habit of adding back pressure to hold altitude [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] becomes "adjust the nose to hold the climb speed" [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

check.q: In a climbing turn your student's airspeed is right on climb speed, but the VSI shows less than in the straight climb. She wants to raise the nose. What do you say?
check.a: Leave it. At constant power the airplane climbs a little more shallowly in a bank because some lift is turning it [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. The airspeed is primary for pitch and it is on target [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]; raising the nose would only cost airspeed.

chunks.title: Leveling off from a climb: the 10 percent lead

body.p: **A level-off from a straight climb.** To level off and hold an altitude, start before reaching it. The lead varies with the rate of climb and pilot technique; an airplane climbing at 1,000 fpm keeps climbing at a decreasing rate through the transition. An effective practice is to lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed: 500 fpm, a 50-foot lead; 1,000 fpm, a 100-foot lead [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

The glass section gives the same rule (1,000 fpm ÷ 10 = 100 feet) and the reason: with no pitch change until the altitude, momentum carries the airplane past it, so a higher vertical speed needs a larger lead [[23:209|IFH 7-48]]. The AFH uses the same 10 percent for visual climbs [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

body.p: Figure 7-29 tags the level-off at cruise: the altimeter is primary for pitch, the heading indicator primary for bank, and the ASI becomes primary for power as the airspeed approaches the desired value [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

**Why hold climb power?** Once the pitch is lowered at the altitude, the excess power that was climbing the airplane accelerates it; reducing power too soon after level-off makes it take longer to accelerate [[23:87|IFH 4-10]]. The AFH adds that lowering the pitch too rapidly, without letting the airspeed build in proportion, can lose altitude [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

**After the level-off.** Trim, and keep an accelerated cross-check until positively established in straight-and-level flight [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. After the first level-off from a climb, check that the attitude indicator shows level at normal cruise and adjust the miniature aircraft if needed [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

**A level-off from a climbing turn.** The IFH airplane sections give no separate procedure; they say only to combine the climb and turn techniques [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. The IFH helicopter chapter says the level-off from a climbing or descending turn is the same as from a straight climb or descent, and that the turn can be stopped first, the level-off made first, or both done together [[23:238|IFH 8-15]]. Application: for an airplane, teach one order. As the bank comes off, vertical lift returns, so the pitch must come down a little more to stay level [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

callout.text: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can create the inversion illusion, a feeling of tumbling backward, and the disoriented pilot may push abruptly nose-low [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Application: a smooth level-off that starts at the right lead is also the prevention.

check.q: Climbing at 800 fpm to 7,000 feet, your student wants cruise speed at the top. Where does she start the level-off, and what does she do with the power?
check.a: Lead by 10 percent of 800 fpm, 80 feet: start at 6,920 [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Keep climb power while the airplane accelerates and reduce to cruise power as the airspeed approaches cruise; the lead depends on how fast it accelerates [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

chunks.title: Entering the descent, from cruise or descent speed

body.p: **Procedure for an entry into a straight descent** on round dials. The IFH method works with or without an attitude indicator: first reduce airspeed to the selected descent airspeed while holding straight-and-level flight, then make a further power reduction to a predetermined setting. As the power is adjusted, lower the nose to hold the airspeed constant, and trim off the pressures [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

**On a PFD** the steps are the same. Reduce power and let the airplane slow in level flight; as it approaches the descent airspeed, reduce power to a predetermined value. Unless the pitch is lowered at the same time, the airspeed keeps decreasing below the target. The ASI tape is primary for pitch: make small corrections on the attitude indicator, confirm them on the airspeed tape, use the airspeed trend indicator, and trim [[23:210|IFH 7-49]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

body.p: The AFH calls the normal partial-power descent a cruise or en route descent: the POH/AFM airspeed and power for a prolonged descent, a target rate of 500 fpm, and a preselected airspeed, pitch attitude and power combination held constant [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Application: when the student must stay at cruise speed, reduce power to the planned setting and lower the nose at the same pace so the airspeed does not move.

**Entry into a descending turn.** Combine the straight descent technique with the turn technique, allow for lift and power when choosing the power setting, and speed up the cross-check [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

**Coordination as the power comes off.** As thrust decreases, speed up the cross-check and be ready with rudder and aileron the instant the instruments show a deviation; effective torque control means countering yaw with rudder pressure [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

callout.text: A rapid deceleration from a quick throttle reduction can lead a disoriented pilot to pull into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Application: teach a smooth power reduction from the very first descent.

check.q: From cruise, your student pulls the power to the descent setting and lowers the nose to a guessed picture at once; the airspeed rises 15 knots. What does the IFH method do differently, and what fixes the speed now?
check.a: The IFH method slows to the descent airspeed in level flight first, then reduces power further and lowers the nose only enough to hold that airspeed, and trims [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Now: the airspeed is high, so the pitch has lowered too far; raise it slightly [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: The stabilized descent, straight and turning

body.p: **A stabilized straight descent.** During a constant airspeed descent, any deviation from the desired airspeed calls for a pitch adjustment [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. On a PFD the ASI tape is primary for pitch; make small corrections on the attitude indicator and validate them on the airspeed tape [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

During the transition the altimeter keeps showing a descent while the airplane settles at a constant airspeed and rate. Hold the pitch constant and let it stabilize; trim continuously through any change in attitude or airspeed, and scan faster while the flightpath and speed are changing [[23:210|IFH 7-49]].

**The rate comes from the power.** Before moving anything, cross-check both airspeed and vertical speed, since a change in one may correct the other [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. In a trimmed airplane the rate of descent is directly proportionate to the thrust removed [[24:369|AFH 18-20]].

body.p: **A stabilized descending turn.** Combine the techniques, consider lift and power when choosing the power setting, and keep the faster cross-check for bank and pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. As the bank increases the vertical lift component decreases [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Application: at the same power and airspeed, expect the descent rate to grow a little in the turn; hold the airspeed with pitch and change power only if the rate matters.

callout.text: Figure 7-30 is captioned "Constant airspeed descent, airspeed high, reduce power," but its tags show the VSI as primary pitch and the ASI as primary power, the constant rate assignment in the text just before it [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:179|IFH 7-18]]. If a student brings it up, use it to show the difference between the two methods.

In a prolonged, coordinated, constant-rate turn the pilot feels no turn; one who notices the altitude loss and pulls back tightens the spiral, the graveyard spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. A long descending turn under the hood is that setup, so keep the student's scan on the turn coordinator and the airspeed.

check.q: In a descending turn at the planned 90 knots, the VSI shows 700 fpm instead of 500. Your student raises the nose. What happens, and what do you teach?
check.a: The airspeed drops below 90: in a constant airspeed descent, pitch is for the airspeed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Cross-check both airspeed and VSI before adjusting [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]; with the speed right, a little more power reduces the rate [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. In a bank the vertical lift is lower [[23:181|IFH 7-20]], so some extra rate is expected.

chunks.title: Leveling off from a descent: three leads

body.p: Reading the figures: in Figure 7-31 the VSI stays primary for pitch, holding the descent rate, with a tag at the altimeter to add power at a 100 to 150 foot lead [[23:179|IFH 7-18]]. In Figure 7-32 the ASI is primary for power and the VSI only supporting pitch, with a tag at the altimeter reading "Primary power at 50' lead"; no instrument is tagged primary for pitch [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

The analog cruise lead looks bigger than 10 percent, but the pitch change itself still starts about 50 feet above at 500 fpm [[23:178|IFH 7-17]], and 50 is 10 percent of 500. Application: the power goes in earlier so the airplane can accelerate while it is still descending. The AFH uses 10 percent for a visual partial-power descent: at 1,000 fpm, start raising the nose and adding power 100 feet above [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
Figure 7-66 shows the glass version: the top image is a power reduction and a 500 fpm descent toward 5,000 feet, the bottom image the power increase that starts the level-off [[23:210|IFH 7-49]].

**A level-off from a descending turn** is the same problem as from a climbing turn: the airplane sections only say to combine the techniques [[23:185|IFH 7-24]], and the climb level-off section above gives the helicopter chapter's three orders [[23:238|IFH 8-15]].

callout.text: **Ballooning** is letting the nose pitch up as power goes in, from not holding the descending attitude with forward pressure [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. It is the classic descent level-off error.

check.q: Descending at 500 fpm to 3,000 feet on round dials, your student will level at cruise speed. Where does she add power, and where does she set the level attitude?
check.a: Cruise power at the 100 to 150 foot lead, between 3,150 and 3,100 feet; then forward pressure to hold 500 fpm until about 50 feet above, 3,050, and smoothly set the level attitude [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Partial panel: climbs and descents without the gyros

body.p: **Procedure using partial panel.** Except the instrument takeoff, every IFH maneuver can be flown with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], and on glass with the AHRS simulated or inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]. The PTS requires Area VI to be taught with full panel and with backup or partial panel instruments (CFII PTS, Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills). FII.VI.A covers recognizing failures and setting them up safely; here is what changes in climbs and descents.

**Why it is harder.** In the transition to a descent, the attitude indicator is the only flight instrument that gives a positive attitude reference. Without it, the ASI, altimeter and VSI show varying rates of change until the airplane settles at a constant airspeed and attitude, so control pressures, trim, cross-check and interpretation must all be accurate [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:210|IFH 7-49]].

body.p: **The airspeed lag.** IFH Chapter 6 says changes in pitch show immediately on the airspeed indicator, with very little lag [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]. The glass section adds a lag that comes from the airplane's momentum, not the instrument: used as the only pitch reference, the airspeed may not show a pitch change in a timely way [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. Partial panel, that tempts the student to stack a second correction on the first. Teach patience: changes do not give instant, stable results, so validate one change before making the next [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

**The compass in climbs and descents.** On a north or south heading, climbing, diving or changing airspeed causes no error; on an east or west heading, acceleration shows a north turn and deceleration a south turn [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. The slowdown before a climb and the speed-up after a level-off both cause it, so read the compass only in steady flight (Application). Timed turns avoid compass errors altogether [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

**Glass partial panel.** In the IFH example an AHRS failure removes all attitude and heading information from the PFD, the slip/skid indicator goes too, and no standby turn coordinator is installed; the airspeed, altimeter and VSI tapes remain [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The standby instruments are an airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Application: the constant airspeed climb keeps its primary pitch instrument, the airspeed tape; bank comes from the standby attitude indicator, and turns are timed.

callout.text: Application: build it up. Start partial panel climbs from climb speed on a north or south heading [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], then add entries from cruise, then level-offs, then climbing and descending turns on the turn coordinator.

check.q: Gyros covered, your student enters a climb from cruise and the airspeed swings 10 knots each side of climb speed. Which IFH facts explain it, and what do you change?
check.a: Without the attitude indicator the airspeed, altimeter and VSI show varying rates until the airplane settles [[23:177|IFH 7-16]], and the airspeed lags pitch changes because of momentum [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. Enter from climb speed, which is easier partial panel [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], and make one small change at a time, validating each [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

chunks.title: Risk: illusions, a lying airspeed indicator and safe practice

body.p: Climbs and descents carry their own spatial disorientation traps:

bullets: **Inversion illusion:** an abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can feel like tumbling backward, and the pilot may push abruptly nose-low [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

**Somatogravic illusion:** a rapid acceleration feels like a nose-up attitude and invites a push nose-low; a quick throttle reduction does the opposite and invites a pull to a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].
**Elevator illusion:** an abrupt upward acceleration in an updraft feels like a climb and invites a push nose-low; a downdraft does the opposite [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

**Graveyard spiral:** in a prolonged, coordinated, constant-rate turn the pilot feels no turn; with no sense of turning, the altitude loss feels like a level descent, and pulling back tightens the spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].
Climbing turns are one of the situations where acceleration forces can overpower gravity and create false sensations [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

body.p: You can let the student feel it. In the IFH "climbing while turning" demonstration, with the student's eyes closed, the instructor flies a slow, well-coordinated turn of about 1.5 G (about 50° of bank) for 90°, which usually feels like a climb; "diving while turning" gives the sensation of diving during the recovery. Do these only with an instructor or safety pilot, and not at low altitude [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

**When the primary pitch instrument lies.** In this Task the airspeed indicator flies the pitch, so a blocked pitot tube matters. If the ram opening and the drain hole are both blocked, the airspeed indicator works like an altimeter as the airplane climbs and descends [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]: it shows more airspeed in a climb and less in a descent [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. A blocked static port shows a decreasing airspeed as the airplane climbs, freezes the altimeter and leaves the VSI on zero [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. Teach the cross-check: a rising airspeed with a steady climb attitude, climb power and a steady VSI does not add up (Application). Pitot tubes can block in visible moisture, which is what pitot heat is for; the POH/AFM has the procedure [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

**Safe practice.** The evaluator will not simulate anything that may jeopardize safe flight (CFII PTS, Introduction); hold yourself to the same rule. Simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot in the other control seat [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], and see and avoid applies under IFR or VFR when weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. Failure to clear the area before and while maneuvering is a typical reason for an unsatisfactory (CFII PTS, Unsatisfactory Performance).

callout.text: Learners should never be allowed to exceed the flight instructor's limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Application: before a descent exercise brief a floor, and before a climb a minimum airspeed; take the controls with the positive exchange at once if either is reached [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Climbing in cloud, your student sees the airspeed creep up while the attitude, climb power and VSI stay the same. She starts raising the nose. What do you suspect, and what do you say?
check.a: A pitot tube blocked at both the ram opening and the drain hole makes the airspeed act like an altimeter, reading higher as the airplane climbs [[23:98|IFH 5-3]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. Stop chasing it: attitude, power and VSI agree, so hold the climb attitude, and use pitot heat per the POH/AFM [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

The IFH lists eleven faults for straight climbs and descents on round dials [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] and ten on glass [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]; they fall under the PTS headings below.

body.p: **How to show them** (Application):

bullets: Torque: enter a climb with your feet flat and let the student watch the heading and ball move, then repeat with right rudder [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

Ballooning: on a descent level-off, add cruise power without forward pressure and let the student see the nose rise; then repeat, holding the descent attitude until about 50 feet above [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].
Trim: after slowing to climb speed, skip the retrim, then relax the back pressure so the student sees the nose drop as the airplane seeks its old trim speed [[23:85|IFH 4-8]].
Slow-speed level-off: level at descent speed by raising the nose first and adding power late, and let the student watch the airspeed fall [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

check.q: The examiner, as your student, levels off from a 500 fpm descent to cruise, and the airplane climbs 80 feet above the altitude as the power comes in. Name the error, the cause and the fix.
check.a: Ballooning: the nose pitched up because he did not hold the descending attitude with forward pressure as power increased [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Fix: add power at the 100 to 150 foot lead and hold forward pressure to keep the rate until about 50 feet above, then level [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Building the lesson and the talk-through

body.p: The telling-and-doing technique fits this Task. First you **demonstrate and simultaneously explain**, giving the power settings and attitudes in the same order you briefed them; if the demonstration strays from the explanation, acknowledge and explain it at once. Then the student tells while you fly, so you can check her understanding before she is busy with the controls [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. When a skill builds on known ones, known to unknown works; when several are taught together, simple to complex [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

Source

Pitch and power together; airspeed primary once stable
2. Straight climb from cruise
Attitude set, power with it or as the speed nears climb speed; trim as the speed falls
3. Level-offs at cruise and at climb speed
10 percent lead; climb power held to accelerate, or pitch and power together
4. Descents and their level-offs
Slow first, set the power, pitch for the airspeed; the 100 to 150 foot and 50 foot leads
5. Climbing and descending turns
Combine with standard-rate turns; faster cross-check
6. Partial panel
Steps 1 to 5 with the gyros covered or the AHRS simulated, starting from climb speed

body.p: Application: the order above follows the AIH's simple-to-complex strategy [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. **Climb from cruise, in primary-and-supporting words** (round dials):

bullets: "Cleared to climb. Heading indicator stays primary for bank [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]."
"Nose up to about the climb picture with light back pressure; the pressure changes as we slow [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]."
"Speed coming down toward climb speed: climb power now, and right rudder for the left-turning tendency [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]."
"VSI trended up and has stopped. Airspeed is primary for pitch now, the tach primary for power. Trimming off the back pressure [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]."
"Two knots slow: a tiny nose-down, then I wait for the result before anything else [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]."
"Climbing 600 to 5,000: I start leveling at 4,940, 10 percent. Forward pressure toward the cruise attitude, climb power until we near cruise speed, then cruise power and trim [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]."

body.p: **Descent, staying at descent speed:**

bullets: "Slowing to descent speed level first. Now power to the descent setting, nose down just enough to hold the speed, and trim [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]."
"Airspeed is primary for pitch: 3 knots fast, so the nose comes up slightly [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]."
"500 down to 3,000: at 3,050 I level the nose and add power to hold this speed, both together [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]."

body.p: **Partial panel version:** "Gyros covered. Entering from climb speed, power and pitch together. Airspeed for pitch, small changes, and I wait for each one. Turn coordinator level, ball centered. Compass only when we are steady [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]] [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]." **In control-and-performance words:** "I set climb power on the tach and the climb attitude on the attitude indicator, trim, cross-check airspeed, VSI and heading, and adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]]."

callout.text: Application: rehearse these scripts aloud under the hood with a safety pilot. The PTS wants the maneuver flown to the instrument pilot skill level while you give effective instruction (CFII PTS, Flight Instructor Responsibility).

check.q: During your climb demo you start the level-off late and overshoot by 60 feet, and say nothing. What should you have done?
check.a: Acknowledge and explain the deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], then fix it in words the student can use: name the rate, the 10 percent lead you missed, and the small correction back down [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

chunks.title: Analyze and correct: when the examiner flies the errors

body.p: For S2 you **analyze and correct simulated common errors**: the evaluator acts as a student during selected maneuvers to see whether you recognize, analyze and correct them (CFII PTS, Introduction). Use the same five steps every time: what you see, the name of the error, its cause, the fix, and a short demonstration if asked.

head: Examiner flies
You say
Source
rows: Climbs 10 knots below climb speed with a big VSI rate
"Airspeed is our pitch instrument here. We're nose-high for this power. Lower the nose a little and let the rate be what it is."
From climb speed, raises the nose and adds power late; the speed sags
"From climb speed, power and pitch go together. Power after the pitch change lets the drag slow us."
Levels off from 800 fpm with no lead; 70 feet high
"No lead. Ten percent of 800 is 80 feet; start there next time. Now a small correction back down."
Pulls power to cruise as soon as the nose is level after a climb
"Power came off too soon, so we'll take longer to reach cruise. Keep climb power until the speed nears cruise."
Adds cruise power at the descent lead without forward pressure; balloons
"Ballooning. Hold the descent attitude with forward pressure as the power comes in, until about 50 feet above."
Holds back pressure through the whole climb
"You're holding pressure. Trim it off, or we can't tell your inputs from the airplane's."
Climb entry with no right rudder; ball out, heading drifting left
"The power and pitch are yawing us left. Right rudder, center the ball, then rudder trim."
Lets the speed decay in a climbing turn at the same bank; the turn coordinator moves past the mark
"Two things: we're slow, so ease the nose down; and the same bank at a lower speed turns faster, so shallow it back to the mark."

body.p: Correcting is not taking over at the first mistake. Safety permitting, let the student go part way into the error and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. When a task needs reteaching, demonstrate it, let the student practice under direction, and evaluate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. If safety requires it, take the controls with the positive exchange [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

callout.text: Application: the examiner may fly two errors at once, such as a late lead and ballooning on the same level-off. Name the one that matters most for safety first, then the other, and give one fix at a time.

check.q: Flying as your student, the examiner levels off at climb speed by lowering the nose but leaving climb power in; the airspeed climbs 15 knots. What do you say?
check.a: Pitch and power did not change together. To level off at climbing airspeed, lower the nose to the level attitude for that speed and reduce power at the same time, in proportion, so the airspeed stays constant [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

scenario.title: Climbing to altitude and back down in a glass trainer
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument student, a private pilot with about 15 hours of hood time, flies the school's fixed-pitch trainer with a PFD and MFD, and a standby airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass. It is a hot summer afternoon with cumulus building, and the radio is busy. Today's plan, in VMC with you as safety pilot: a climb from 2,500 to 6,500 feet with climbing turns, level-offs, then descents, first full panel and then with the AHRS simulated failed.

questions.q: Before engine start, which numbers do you make sure she has, and why?
questions.a: The POH climb airspeed and climb power, descent airspeed and power, and cruise power. The climb speed and power come from the POH/AFM [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], and failure to learn and use proper power settings is a listed error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Remind her the published speeds assume maximum gross weight [[23:207|IFH 7-46]].

questions.q: Climbing out from cruise, she raises the chevron and adds full power. The airspeed settles 12 knots below climb speed with 1,000 fpm showing, and she is pleased. What do you say?
questions.a: Once stable, the airspeed is primary for pitch; it is low, so make small pitch changes, nose down, until it settles on climb speed [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. The rate will drop to whatever the pitch, power, weight and conditions give [[23:207|IFH 7-46]] [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. Then trim, since any change in airspeed requires a trim adjustment [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

questions.q: Passing 5,000 feet in the heat, the climb rate falls to about 400 fpm at climb speed and full throttle. She wants to raise the nose to get 500 back. What do you teach?
questions.a: Hold climb speed: in this Task pitch is for the airspeed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], and the rate depends on weight and atmospheric conditions [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. A normally aspirated engine loses power as it climbs, so check the throttle is at the climb setting [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. On an IFR clearance, if unable to climb at least 500 fpm, advise ATC [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]].

questions.q: At 90 knots you ask for a 90° left climbing turn. She rolls to 25° of bank and stares at the heading. What do you correct?
questions.a: Standard rate at about 90 knots true airspeed is about 13° to 14° of bank by the 15 percent rule [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]], and the turn rate indicator is primary for bank in a standard-rate turn [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. Steep banks cut the climb rate a lot [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. In a 90° standard-rate turn the heading can be left out of the scan for about 20 seconds; staring at it is fixation [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

questions.q: Climbing at 600 fpm to 6,500, she starts the level-off at 6,500 and overshoots 70 feet. Name the error and the fix.
questions.a: Failure to determine a proper lead from the vertical speed [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. Lead by 10 percent: 60 feet, starting at 6,440 [[23:209|IFH 7-48]]. Keep climb power until the speed nears cruise and reduce it before cruise is reached [[23:209|IFH 7-48]].

questions.q: You simulate an AHRS failure for the descent. She asks what she still has and how to start down.
questions.a: In the IFH example the PFD loses attitude, heading and the slip/skid indicator but keeps the airspeed, altitude and VSI tapes [[23:217|IFH 7-56]], and there is a standby airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. The descent entry works with or without an attitude indicator: slow in level flight, reduce to the set power, lower the nose to hold the speed, trim [[23:210|IFH 7-49]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Expect changing values through the transition and keep inputs small [[23:210|IFH 7-49]] [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

skills.do: From the right seat, fly a constant airspeed climb and a constant airspeed descent to the instrument pilot skill level while explaining, in your chosen method's words, the entry from cruise or from climb or descent speed, which instrument is primary once stable, the correction for an airspeed error, the level-off lead, and the power and trim at each step; then repeat it partial panel or on the backup instruments.
skills.practice: Rehearse this lesson's talk-through aloud under the hood with a qualified safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], in the same order you brief it, admitting any deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Drill the leads until you can say the rate and the level-off altitude without thinking [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

skills.do: When the evaluator flies a listed error (pitch used for the rate, a late or missing lead, ballooning, pitch and power out of step on a slow-speed level-off, chasing the VSI, torque not countered, pressures held instead of trimmed), say what you see, name the error, explain the cause, give the fix, and demonstrate it if asked.
skills.practice: Take turns with another applicant flying the IFH climb and descent fault lists for each other [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]], never simulating anything that could jeopardize safe flight (CFII PTS, Introduction).

quiz.q: Your student is in a stabilized constant airspeed climb. The VSI shows a good rate, but the airspeed is 5 knots low. What correction does the IFH call for?
options: Add power until the speed returns
A small pitch decrease
Raise the nose to hold the rate
Retrim nose-up and wait for it
quiz.why: Once stable, the ASI is primary for pitch; if the airspeed is low or high, make an appropriately small pitch correction [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Adding power while holding the vertical speed is the constant rate fix [[23:177|IFH 7-16]], and raising the nose would slow the airplane further [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].

quiz.q: Climbing at 700 fpm to 8,000 feet, at what altitude should your student begin the level-off by the IFH rule?
options: 7,930 feet
7,950 feet
7,900 feet
At 8,000 feet
quiz.why: Lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed: 70 feet, so 7,930 [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. 7,950 would be the lead for 500 fpm, and 7,900 the lead for 1,000 fpm.

quiz.q: From climbing airspeed, your student raises the nose and adds climb power a few seconds later. What will the airspeed do?
options: Rise, from the excess thrust of the late power
Stay the same, since she is already flying at climb speed
Drop, from the added drag before the power comes in
Rise first, then settle back on the climb speed
quiz.why: Power added after the pitch change shows a decrease in airspeed from the increased drag; power added before it makes the airspeed rise from excess thrust [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. From climb speed, power goes up at the same time as the pitch [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

quiz.q: Gyros covered, your student must enter a climb. From which speed does the IFH say the entry is easier and more accurate?
options: From cruise speed, power first
From any speed, if the VSI is primary
From cruise speed, pitch first
From climbing speed
quiz.why: Climb entries on partial panel are more easily and accurately controlled when entering from climbing speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The VSI is primary for pitch only in a constant rate climb once the rate settles [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

quiz.q: Descending at 500 fpm on round dials, your student will level off at a cruise speed higher than her descent speed. When does she add cruise power?
options: About 100 to 150 feet above the altitude
About 50 feet above the altitude
At the altitude, then lower the nose
About 300 feet above the altitude
quiz.why: Assuming 500 fpm, lead by 100 to 150 feet for a level-off at a higher airspeed and add cruise power at the lead point [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. About 50 feet is where she smoothly sets the level attitude, and the lead when staying at descent speed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

quiz.q: During a constant airspeed descent, the airspeed is 5 knots above target with the power as planned. What does the IFH say to change?
options: Add a little more power
Lower the nose for more rate
Raise the pitch attitude slightly
Retrim nose-down for the speed
quiz.why: Any deviation from the desired airspeed calls for a pitch adjustment [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]; a higher airspeed means the pitch attitude has lowered and should be raised [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]. Adding power would only raise the airspeed further. Figure 7-30 is captioned "airspeed high, reduce power," but it is tagged with the constant rate primaries; the text is the rule [[23:179|IFH 7-18]].

quiz.q: As your student adds cruise power to level off from a descent, the nose rises and she climbs back above the target altitude. What does the IFH call this error?
options: Chasing the vertical speed
Ballooning
Failure to lead the airspeed
Overcontrolling on the entry
quiz.why: Ballooning is allowing the nose to pitch up on level-offs from descents, from not holding the descending attitude with forward pressure as power is increased [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

quiz.q: On a PFD, your student levels off from a 1,000 fpm descent and returns to cruise. What does the glass section of the IFH say to do?
options: Start 50 feet above; raise the pitch, then add the power
Start 150 feet above; pitch and power at the same time
Start 300 feet above; hold the rate until the altitude
Start 100 feet above; cruise power first, then the pitch
quiz.why: Lead by 10 percent of the rate, 100 feet at 1,000 fpm, and increase power to cruise before increasing the pitch toward level [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Raising pitch before adding power adds drag and loses airspeed [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

quiz.q: Your student, climbing straight at climb power and climb speed, rolls into a 20° bank and keeps the climb speed. What should she expect?
options: A slightly shallower climb
A steeper climb from the bank
A rising airspeed in the turn
No change if the ball is centered
quiz.why: At constant power the same pitch and airspeed cannot be held in a bank as in a straight climb; the airplane climbs at a slightly shallower angle because some lift is turning it, and steep banks cut the rate a lot [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

quiz.q: Look at the two panels. Which instrument is primary for pitch in the stabilized constant airspeed climb (top), and which in the constant rate climb (bottom)?
options: VSI on top, airspeed on the bottom
Attitude indicator on top, altimeter below
Airspeed on top, VSI on the bottom
Altimeter on top, VSI on the bottom
quiz.why: Once a constant airspeed climb is stable the ASI is primary for pitch; in a constant rate climb the VSI becomes primary for pitch once it stabilizes and the ASI primary for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The figure tags show the same [[23:176|IFH 7-15]].

quiz.q: Gyros covered, heading 090, your student slows from cruise to climb speed before a climb, and the compass swings toward south. What do you teach?
options: Bank left to stop the compass swinging toward the south
Turn coordinator level; it is only deceleration error
Start a timed turn back to 090 using the clock
Bank right, since the compass lags on east headings
quiz.why: On an east or west heading, deceleration gives a south-turn indication [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Keep the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft level with the ball centered [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] and read the compass in steady flight.

quiz.q: On every climb entry your student's heading drifts left as the power comes up and the nose rises, and the ball moves off center. What is the most likely cause?
options: A heading indicator that precesses in climbs
Too little power for the chosen climb attitude
Nose-up trim set before the power was added
Torque and P-factor not met with right rudder
quiz.why: Added power makes the airplane yaw and roll left unless aileron and rudder counter it [[23:170|IFH 7-9]], and in a climb P-factor and torque need right rudder and aileron [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Trim the ball with rudder trim toward the displaced side [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

quiz.q: Your glass student corrects a low climb airspeed with a small pitch change, sees no change for two seconds, and starts another. What does the IFH tell her?
options: Make a bigger change so it shows sooner
Wait until the first change is validated
Switch to the VSI as primary pitch
Add power, since pitch has not worked
quiz.why: Changes do not produce instantaneous, stabilized results; avoid rushing into another change until the first is validated [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. The airspeed lags pitch changes because of momentum [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. The VSI is primary for pitch only in a constant rate climb [[23:209|IFH 7-48]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the IFH tell the pilot to keep climb power for a while after starting a level-off to cruise airspeed?
options: So it speeds up to cruise; power comes off as cruise nears
So the nose does not drop as the airspeed falls off at the level-off
So the vertical speed holds steady until the target altitude
So the engine cools before the power is finally reduced
final_quiz.why: Hold climb power while the airspeed increases and reduce to cruise as it approaches cruise; the lead depends on the rate of acceleration [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Reducing power too soon after level-off makes acceleration take longer [[23:87|IFH 4-10]].

final_quiz.q: Leveling off at climbing airspeed, your student lowers the nose but reduces power several seconds later. What does the airspeed do?
options: It drops from the added drag
It rises until the power comes off
It stays the same; only pitch changed
It drops, then recovers with the power
final_quiz.why: To level off at climbing airspeed, lower the nose and reduce power at the same time; if the reduction is proportionate to the pitch change, the airspeed stays constant [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. With the pitch lowered at climb power, the excess power accelerates the airplane [[23:87|IFH 4-10]].

final_quiz.q: Descending at descent speed, your student will stay at that speed after the level-off. What lead and technique does the IFH give?
options: About 150 feet; add power first, then level the pitch
About 10 feet; level the pitch, then add power later
About 50 feet; pitch to level and add power together
About 100 feet; hold the rate down to the altitude
final_quiz.why: Lead the altitude by about 50 feet, at the same time adjusting the pitch to level flight and adding power to a setting that holds the airspeed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: On a PFD, which instrument does the IFH make primary for pitch in a constant airspeed descent?
options: The VSI tape
The altitude tape
The attitude indicator
The airspeed tape
final_quiz.why: The primary instrument for pitch is the ASI tape; in a constant rate descent it is the VSI tape [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. On glass the attitude indicator is primary only when flying a specific pitch or bank angle [[23:199|IFH 7-38]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about the airspeed indicator as a pitch instrument does the IFH support?
options: It shows pitch directly, like the attitude indicator
It cannot be used for pitch once the power is set
It may lag a pitch change because of momentum
It reacts to pitch changes faster than any other
final_quiz.why: The ASI gives an indirect indication of pitch [[23:167|IFH 7-6]], and used as the sole pitch reference it may not show a pitch change in a timely way because of momentum [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. In this maneuver, with power set, it is primary for pitch [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

final_quiz.q: In a constant airspeed descent, your student is on the planned airspeed but sees 700 fpm instead of the 500 she planned. What do you coach?
options: Add a little power; keep the speed with pitch
Raise the nose until the VSI shows 500 fpm
Lower the nose and reduce power together
Retrim nose-up so the rate slows down
final_quiz.why: In a trimmed airplane the descent rate is directly proportionate to the thrust removed [[24:369|AFH 18-20]], and in a constant airspeed descent pitch is for the airspeed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Cross-check both before adjusting [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Raising the nose would cost airspeed.

final_quiz.q: Your student holds back pressure through the whole climb instead of trimming. Why does the IFH call that an error?
options: Trim is needed only at the level-off, not before
Held pressure makes the airspeed indicator lag
The VSI will not settle until the airplane is trimmed
She cannot tell her own inputs from the airplane's
final_quiz.why: Unless the airplane is trimmed, it is hard to tell whether control pressure changes come from aerodynamic changes or from the pilot's own movements [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Trim also lets her hold a new pitch and validate a correction [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

final_quiz.q: Your student keeps raising the nose to hold 700 fpm as the airspeed bleeds off below climb speed. What do you tell her?
options: Good: the VSI is the primary pitch instrument in climbs
Pitch holds the airspeed here; take the rate it gives
Add power until 700 fpm returns at this attitude
Hold this attitude and trim until the speed settles
final_quiz.why: In a constant airspeed climb the ASI is primary for pitch once stable [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], and the rate depends on weight and atmospheric conditions [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. The VSI is primary for pitch only in a constant rate climb [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

final_quiz.q: ATC clears your IFR student from 3,000 to 9,000 feet with no restrictions and no "pilot's discretion." What does the AIM expect?
options: 500 fpm all the way, then 300 fpm at the end
Any rate, with temporary level-offs allowed
Optimum rate all the way, reporting every 1,000
Optimum rate to 8,000, then 500 to 1,500 fpm
final_quiz.why: Climb at an optimum rate to 1,000 feet below the assigned altitude, then at 500 to 1,500 fpm, and advise ATC if unable to climb at least 500 fpm [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]. Any rate with temporary level-offs describes a pilot's discretion clearance [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]].

final_quiz.q: In a climbing turn on a PFD, which instrument does the IFH make primary for bank to hold a standard-rate turn?
options: The attitude indicator's roll scale
The heading indicator
The turn rate indicator
The slip/skid indicator
final_quiz.why: The turn rate indicator is the primary bank instrument because it is the only one that can specifically show a standard-rate turn; the attitude indicator sets the bank and supports [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

final_quiz.q: In a climb in cloud, the airspeed slowly rises while the attitude, climb power and VSI stay the same. What could explain it?
options: A pitot tube blocked at the ram opening and drain hole
A static port blocked while the pitot tube stays clear
Normal airspeed lag from the airplane's momentum
Carburetor ice slowly reducing the engine's power output
final_quiz.why: With the ram opening and drain hole blocked, the ASI acts like an altimeter [[23:98|IFH 5-3]] and shows more airspeed as the airplane climbs [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. A blocked static port shows a decreasing airspeed in a climb [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]], and lost power would lower the speed.

final_quiz.q: Your student flies a perfect constant airspeed climb under the hood. How do you check that she understands the maneuver, not just the picture?
options: Have her vary it or combine it with a turn or a level-off
Have her repeat the same climb ten times on one heading
Ask her to recite the IFH error list from memory
Move on, since she flew it well the first time
final_quiz.why: A learner who performs a maneuver correctly may not understand it; have her vary it slightly or combine it with other operations [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Repeating one drill improves short-term performance but can fool both of you [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

final_quiz.q: Which IFH illusion is tied most closely to an abrupt level-off from a climb?
options: The graveyard spiral
The inversion illusion
The elevator illusion
The false horizon illusion
final_quiz.why: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can create the illusion of tumbling backward, the inversion illusion; the pilot may push abruptly nose-low [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. The elevator illusion comes from an updraft or downdraft [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

final_quiz.q: In the IFH example AHRS failure, what does your glass student still have for a constant airspeed climb?
options: The PFD attitude and heading, without the slip/skid indicator
Airspeed, altitude and VSI tapes, plus the standby instruments
Only the standby airspeed indicator and the altimeter
The full PFD, with the autopilot flying the pitch
final_quiz.why: An AHRS failure removes attitude and heading from the PFD and the slip/skid indicator; the airspeed, altitude and VSI tapes remain [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The standby group is an airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. The autopilot keeps only roll and altitude hold [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

final_quiz.q: Flying as your student, the examiner levels off at descent speed by raising the nose first and adding power later; the airspeed sags 8 knots. Name the error.
options: Ballooning from too little forward pressure
Failure to vary the rate of the cross-check
Uncoordinated pitch and power on level-off
Chasing the VSI during the transition
final_quiz.why: Pitch and power need to change in unison at level-off; increasing pitch before adding power generates drag and lowers the airspeed [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. The analog list calls it improper pitch and power coordination on slow-speed level-offs [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Ballooning is a nose-up on the power increase.

final_quiz.q: Why does the IFH say to check the attitude indicator after the first level-off from a climb?
options: To see whether the gyro precessed during the climb
To set the climb attitude mark for the next climb
To confirm the suction is normal at the new altitude
To set the miniature aircraft for level cruise
final_quiz.why: Following the initial level-off from a climb, check the attitude indicator and adjust the miniature aircraft for a level indication at normal cruise [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]; it is set at cruise and not changed for other speeds [[23:138|IFH 6-5]].

final_quiz.q: In a climbing turn at 90 knots true airspeed, about what bank gives a standard-rate turn by the IFH 15 percent rule of thumb?
options: About 14°
About 9°
About 18°
About 30°
final_quiz.why: 15 percent of true airspeed: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, plus half of 9 = 13.5°, about 14° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. 18° is the figure for 120 knots [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. The other IFH rule, airspeed ÷ 10 plus 7, would give 16° [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], which is why the question names the rule.

takeaways: Constant airspeed: the power is set, pitch holds the airspeed, and the rate is what the airplane gives.
Once stable: airspeed primary for pitch, heading for bank, tach or manifold pressure for power.
From climb speed, power and pitch go together; from cruise, power with the pitch or as the speed nears climb speed.
Descents: slow in level flight, set the predetermined power, lower the nose to hold the speed, trim.
Leads: 10 percent of the climb rate; at 500 fpm down, power at 100 to 150 feet for cruise, about 50 feet at descent speed; 10 percent on glass.
Leveling at climb or descent speed: pitch and power together. Leveling to cruise: let the power accelerate you and hold the nose against ballooning.
Partial panel: enter from climb speed, use small inputs, and wait for the airspeed to catch up.
For every error: what you see, its name, its cause, the fix and how you would show it.
cfi_notes: The sources give several level-off leads. Climbs: 10 percent of the vertical speed on round dials [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] and on glass [[23:209|IFH 7-48]]. Descents on round dials: 100 to 150 feet at 500 fpm for a level-off at a higher airspeed, about 50 feet at descent speed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Descents on glass: 10 percent [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. The AFH uses 10 percent for climbs and partial-power descents [[24:81|AFH 3-20]] [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Read together, the pitch change starts near 10 percent in each (about 50 feet at 500 fpm); the round-dial method to cruise simply adds the power earlier, at 100 to 150 feet. This comparison is an interpretation; no source makes it.

Order of power and pitch when leveling from a descent to cruise: round dials add power at the lead and hold forward pressure until about 50 feet above [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]; glass says increase power to cruise before raising the pitch [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Both put power first. At climb or descent speed, both change pitch and power together [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

Climb power timing from cruise: the analog section allows power with the pitch change or after the pitch is set [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]; the glass section allows it before the pitch change or after [[23:207|IFH 7-46]]; the AFH visual climb adds power while raising the nose [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. From climb speed all agree on together [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. Teach one way and say why.

Figure and text disagree in three places: Figure 7-25 tags no primary pitch instrument for the entry [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]; Figure 7-30 is captioned a constant airspeed descent but tagged with the constant rate primaries [[23:179|IFH 7-18]]; Figure 7-64 tags primary power at the airspeed tape and primary pitch at the altitude tape, not the stabilized-climb primaries in the text on the same page [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]; its 100 knots, 4,000 feet and 18 inches match the level slowdown that starts the entry, which the IFH tags the same way [[23:201|IFH 7-40]]. Teach the text, and be ready to explain the pictures.

Airspeed lag: IFH 6-6 says there is very little lag in the airspeed indicator [[23:139|IFH 6-6]], while IFH 7-37 says the airspeed may not show a pitch change in a timely way because of momentum [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. They describe different things, the instrument and the airplane; the second matters most partial panel, when the airspeed is the only pitch reference.

Level-offs from climbing and descending turns are described only in the IFH helicopter chapter [[23:238|IFH 8-15]]; the airplane sections say only to combine the techniques [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. If the examiner asks, say so, and teach one order consistently.

The AFH emergency climb and descent for a VFR pilot in IMC (no more than one bar width, accept whatever climb speed results, power in 100 rpm steps, no more than 500 fpm down) is a different procedure from this Task [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Students who learned it as private pilots may bring the habit; always name the procedure being flown.

The PTS references FAA-H-8083-9 and FAA-H-8083-15 without suffixes; teach from the current AIH (8083-9B) and IFH (8083-15B). The PTS names the view-limiting device for Task H and the nonprecision approach (CFII PTS, Introduction); for this Task, agree with the examiner beforehand whether you will wear one.

Expect questions on which instrument is primary for pitch on entry and once stable, the level-off leads and the difference from constant rate, and expect the examiner to fly pitch-for-rate, ballooning and a no-lead level-off as your student. The evaluator must also cause a realistic distraction during the flight (CFII PTS, Use of Distractions During Practical Tests).
gaps: Climb and descent airspeeds, power settings, pitch attitudes and trim feel for your airplane come from the POH/AFM and your own flying; the IFH uses sample airplanes [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:207|IFH 7-46]].
The CFII PTS gives no numeric tolerances for this Task; it asks for the instrument pilot skill level. The Instrument Rating ACS tolerances are not in these build sources.
No airplane section of the IFH gives a procedure for leveling off from a climbing or descending turn; only the helicopter chapter does [[23:238|IFH 8-15]].
No source adjusts the level-off leads for partial panel flight or for the lag of an analog VSI; the leads are rules of thumb for normal flight.
No source gives a minimum altitude for practicing descents under the hood; the IFH says only that disorientation demonstrations should not be done at low altitudes [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].
No source gives descent power settings for a given rate in a typical trainer; the AFH says only to use the POH/AFM numbers with a 500 fpm target for a cruise descent [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

activities.title: Constant airspeed or constant rate?
activities.intro: Tap each statement, then tap the method it belongs to.

activities.title: Leveling off from a climb to cruise speed
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Note the vertical speed and set a lead of 10 percent of it
At the lead, apply smooth, steady forward pressure toward the level attitude
Watch the VSI move toward zero, the altimeter slow and the airspeed build
Hold climb power as the airplane accelerates, correcting pitch and torque
Reduce to cruise power as the airspeed approaches cruise
Trim, and keep a fast cross-check until established in level flight
activities.why: Lead and level-off sequence [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]; accelerated cross-check until positively established in straight-and-level flight [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

activities.title: Leads, banks and timing
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Climbing at 900 fpm to 6,000 feet, at what altitude should the level-off begin by the IFH rule?
On a PFD, descending at 800 fpm to return to cruise, how many feet of lead does the IFH rule give?
items.why: 10 percent of the rate of descent: 800 ÷ 10 = 80 feet [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

items.q: Round dials, descending at 500 fpm to 4,000 feet to level at cruise speed. At the earliest, at what altitude does the IFH lead have the student add cruise power?
items.why: The lead is 100 to 150 feet at 500 fpm, so the earliest point is 4,000 + 150 = 4,150 feet [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

items.q: Same descent: at about what altitude does she smoothly set the level attitude?
items.why: Hold forward pressure to keep the descent rate until about 50 feet above the altitude: 4,050 [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

items.q: In a climbing turn at 110 knots true airspeed, about what bank gives a standard-rate turn by the IFH 15 percent rule of thumb?
Cleared from 2,000 to 7,000 feet with no restrictions, at what altitude does the AIM expect the climb to change from optimum rate to 500 to 1,500 fpm?
items.why: Climb at an optimum rate to 1,000 feet below the assigned altitude, then 500 to 1,500 fpm: 7,000 - 1,000 = 6,000 [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]].

activities.title: True or false: partial panel and risk
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The IFH says climb entries on partial panel are more easily controlled from climbing speed than from cruise.
The IFH descent entry method only works with a working attitude indicator.
cards.why: False. The method of slowing in level flight, then reducing to a set power and lowering the nose, is effective with or without an attitude indicator [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

cards.s: Used as the only pitch reference, the airspeed indicator may not show a pitch change in a timely way.
cards.why: True. The lag comes from the airplane's momentum, not the instrument [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

cards.s: If the pitot tube's ram opening and drain hole are both blocked, the airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter as the airplane climbs and descends.
cards.why: True [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. It shows more airspeed in a climb and less in a descent [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

cards.s: With the eyes closed, a slow, well-coordinated turn usually feels like a descent.
cards.why: False. The usual illusion in the climbing-while-turning demonstration is a climb [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

cards.s: After an AHRS failure in the IFH example, the slip/skid indicator is still shown on the PFD.
cards.why: False. The slip/skid indicator is lost, and no standby turn coordinator is installed [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

activities.title: A climb and descent lesson, one call at a time
activities.intro: Your instrument student flies a fixed-pitch six-pack trainer. It is VMC and you are the safety pilot.

steps.s: On the ground she asks which instrument tells her the pitch is right once the climb is stable.
options: The airspeed indicator, with the power set
The VSI, since it shows the climb directly
The altimeter, as in level flight
The attitude indicator, since it shows pitch
steps.why: Once stable at a constant airspeed and attitude, the ASI is primary for pitch [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The VSI is primary for pitch only in a constant rate climb [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

steps.s: On the climb entry from cruise, the heading drifts left as the power comes up and the nose rises, with the ball out to the right.
options: Left aileron to stop the drift and level the wings
Less power so the yaw goes away on its own
Right rudder to center the ball, then rudder trim
Nothing: it will settle once the speed is steady
steps.why: Power and a higher pitch yaw and roll the airplane left; right rudder and aileron counter it [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Step on the ball [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]], and use rudder trim in the direction the ball is displaced [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

steps.s: Climbing at 500 fpm to 4,000 feet, she says she will level off when the altimeter reads 4,000.
options: Fine, the airplane stops climbing at once
Start at 3,950: 10 percent of the rate
Start at 3,900 to leave a margin
Start at 3,800, a 200-foot lead
steps.why: Lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed: 500 fpm, a 50-foot lead [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. The airplane keeps climbing at a decreasing rate through the transition [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

steps.s: For the descent she pulls the power from cruise and lowers the nose at once, and the airspeed rises 15 knots.
options: Let it go, since speed does not matter in a descent
Add a little power so she can keep the nose low
Have her trim nose-down to suit the new speed
Level first to slow, then set power and pitch for speed
steps.why: The IFH entry: reduce to the descent airspeed in level flight, then reduce power further and lower the nose to hold the airspeed constant [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

steps.s: Descending at 500 fpm to level at cruise, she adds cruise power 120 feet above and the nose starts to rise.
options: Hold forward pressure and the rate until 50 feet above
Pull the power back off until the nose settles down
Let the nose rise, since that is the level-off starting
Trim nose-up to match the new, higher power setting
steps.why: The nose tends to rise as the airspeed increases; hold forward pressure to keep the descent rate until about 50 feet above, then set the level attitude [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Not doing so is ballooning [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

steps.s: In the debrief, how do you assess her?
options: Grade the whole flight as satisfactory or not
Read her the IFH error list and score her on it
Her self-assessment, then yours, element by element
Wait until her stage check to discuss the flight
steps.why: Collaborative assessment: learner self-assessment, then a discussion comparing it with the instructor's assessment, judged against standards for her stage and element by element [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
